title: CUDA and parallel programming
text:
CHAPTER 15. GPUS AND THE COMPUTE REVOLUTION
SECTION 15.2. CUDA AND PARALLEL PROGRAMMING

Section 15.1 showed how researchers forced graphics hardware to compute by pretending their data were textures and their programs were pixel shaders. CUDA ended the pretending. Released by Nvidia in 2007, it let programmers write ordinary C-like code that runs on thousands of GPU threads, with direct access to memory. Within a few years it had become the standard platform for scientific GPU computing and then for deep learning, and Nvidia's lead in AI hardware rests heavily on the software ecosystem built on it. This section explains the CUDA programming model, the GPU memory hierarchy, the key optimization of tiling for matrix multiplication, and the libraries that made GPUs usable for neural networks.

1. Origins

CUDA (originally "Compute Unified Device Architecture") was developed at Nvidia from 2004 by a team including Ian Buck (who had created BrookGPU at Stanford) and John Nickolls. The initial CUDA SDK was made public on 15 February 2007 for Windows and Linux, supporting the G80-generation GPUs (GeForce 8800 and related cards) whose unified processors were designed with general computing in mind. Nickolls, Buck, Michael Garland and Kevin Skadron described the model in "Scalable Parallel Programming with CUDA" (ACM Queue, 2008). Nvidia also launched the Tesla product line of GPUs for computing without display outputs.

Alternatives followed: OpenCL, an open standard managed by the Khronos Group (version 1.0 in 2008-2009, initially proposed by Apple), runs on GPUs from several vendors and on CPUs; AMD later built ROCm and HIP, a CUDA-like interface. But CUDA's head start, tools, libraries and performance made it dominant in machine learning.

2. The programming model: grids, blocks, threads

A CUDA program has host code (runs on the CPU) and kernels (functions that run on the GPU). Launching a kernel starts a grid of thread blocks; each block contains up to 1024 threads (on current hardware); every thread runs the same kernel code but has its own indices to decide which data to process.

Vector addition, the "hello world":

    __global__ void add(const float *a, const float *b, float *c, int n)
    {
        int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // global thread index
        if (i < n)
            c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
    }

    // host side
    int threads = 256;
    int blocks = (n + threads - 1) / threads;   // round up
    add<<<blocks, threads>>>(d_a, d_b, d_c, n);

With n = 1,000,000 and 256 threads per block, this launches 3,907 blocks, about a million threads, one per element. (The comments use C++ "//" syntax; they are part of the code, not formatting.) The "if (i < n)" guard handles the last, partially filled block. The host must also allocate GPU memory (cudaMalloc), copy inputs to it (cudaMemcpy), and copy results back.

Why blocks? Threads within a block run on the same streaming multiprocessor (SM), can share a fast on-chip memory (shared memory) and can synchronize with a barrier (__syncthreads()). Threads in different blocks cannot synchronize directly during a kernel. This restriction lets the hardware schedule blocks on any SM in any order, so the same program scales automatically from a small GPU with a few SMs to a large one with over a hundred: the "scalable" in the 2008 paper's title.

3. Warps and SIMT execution

The hardware executes threads in groups of 32 called warps. All threads in a warp execute the same instruction at the same time on different data (single instruction, multiple threads, SIMT). Consequences:

  - Branch divergence: if threads in a warp take different sides of an if statement, the warp executes both paths one after the other, with some threads masked off. Code where all 32 threads take the same path runs at full speed.
  - Latency hiding: each SM holds many warps at once. When one warp waits hundreds of cycles for global memory, the scheduler issues instructions from another ready warp. Enough warps in flight ("occupancy") keep the arithmetic units busy. This is the throughput design of Section 15.1.

4. The memory hierarchy

Performance in CUDA is mostly about data movement. The main memory spaces, from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest:

  - Registers: private to each thread; fastest.
  - Shared memory: on-chip, per block, tens to a few hundred kilobytes per SM; latency of a few tens of cycles; explicitly managed by the programmer.
  - L1 and L2 caches: hardware-managed.
  - Global memory: the GPU's DRAM (GDDR or HBM), gigabytes to tens of gigabytes; hundreds of cycles of latency, but very high bandwidth when accessed well.
  - Host memory: CPU RAM across the PCI Express bus (or faster links like NVLink); much slower than GPU memory. Minimizing host-GPU transfers is a first rule of GPU programming.

Memory coalescing: when the 32 threads of a warp access consecutive addresses, the hardware combines them into a few wide memory transactions. Scattered accesses waste bandwidth. So data layout (for example, "structure of arrays" rather than "array of structures") strongly affects speed.

5. Tiled matrix multiplication

Matrix multiplication C = A B (all n x n) is the core operation of neural networks. A naive kernel assigns one thread per element of C:

    __global__ void matmul_naive(const float *A, const float *B, float *C, int n)
    {
        int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
        int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
        if (row < n && col < n) {
            float sum = 0.0f;
            for (int k = 0; k < n; k++)
                sum += A[row * n + k] * B[k * n + col];
            C[row * n + col] = sum;
        }
    }

Each thread reads 2n values from global memory to do 2n floating-point operations: arithmetic intensity of about 2n FLOPs per 8n bytes = 0.25 FLOP per byte. That is memory-bound (Section 15.1), far below the roofline knee of a modern GPU, which needs tens of FLOPs per byte or more.

But each element of A is used by n different threads (all threads in the same row of C), and each element of B by n threads. Tiling exploits that reuse. Divide the matrices into T x T tiles (say T = 16 or 32). Each block computes one T x T tile of C. It loops over the tiles along k:

    for each tile index t along the k dimension:
        all threads in the block cooperatively load one T x T tile of A
            and one T x T tile of B from global memory into shared memory
        __syncthreads()      // wait until the tiles are loaded
        each thread accumulates T products from the shared tiles
        __syncthreads()      // wait before overwriting the tiles

Now each element loaded from global memory is used T times from fast shared memory, so global memory traffic falls by a factor of T, and arithmetic intensity rises by T: for T = 32, from 0.25 to about 8 FLOPs per byte, and more with additional register-level tiling (each thread computing several outputs). Production libraries go further with multiple levels of tiling (registers, shared memory, L2), double buffering (loading the next tile while computing on the current one), and hardware matrix units, reaching a large fraction of peak performance.

This is the same idea as cache blocking on CPUs (Section 6.4) and as the systolic arrays of Section 6.4, which Google's TPU accelerators use for matrix multiplication: reuse data close to the arithmetic.

6. Libraries: why researchers rarely write kernels

Most deep learning researchers never write CUDA kernels; they use libraries:

  - cuBLAS: Nvidia's implementation of BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), the standard interface for vector and matrix operations defined from the late 1970s onward. Its GEMM (general matrix multiply) routine is the workhorse of neural network computation.
  - cuDNN: a library of deep neural network primitives (convolutions, pooling, normalization, activation functions, recurrent layers), described in "cuDNN: Efficient Primitives for Deep Learning" (Sharan Chetlur and colleagues, arXiv, October 2014). It offers several algorithms for each convolution (direct, lowering to matrix multiply via "im2col," FFT-based, Winograd) and picks fast ones.
  - cuFFT, cuSPARSE, cuRAND and others for FFTs, sparse matrices and random numbers.
  - NCCL (Nvidia Collective Communications Library): fast all-reduce and other collective operations for training across many GPUs.

Deep learning frameworks were built on these: Theano (Montreal, from 2007), Caffe (Berkeley, 2013), Torch (Lua), TensorFlow (Google, 2015), PyTorch (Facebook, 2016), JAX (Google). A framework user writes "y = x @ W" in Python; the framework calls cuBLAS; automatic differentiation (Section 13.1) creates the backward pass, which is again matrix multiplications. When AlexNet was trained in 2012 (Chapter 16), Alex Krizhevsky wrote his own CUDA convolution code ("cuda-convnet"); within a few years such code was packaged into libraries that anyone could use.

Lowering convolution to matrix multiplication (im2col): for each output position, copy the input patch it depends on (k x k x C_in values) into a column of a large matrix. Then all outputs are computed by one big matrix multiplication of the kernel matrix (C_out rows by k*k*C_in columns) with this patch matrix. This wastes memory (each input pixel is copied up to k^2 times) but converts convolution into a highly optimized GEMM.

7. Programming beyond CUDA C

Writing efficient GPU kernels by hand is hard, so higher-level tools have spread:

  - Compilers inside frameworks fuse operations (for example, a matrix multiply followed by a bias add and activation) into a single kernel to avoid writing intermediate results to memory. Kernel fusion matters because many operations in neural networks (element-wise activations, normalization) are memory-bound.
  - Triton (Philippe Tillet's doctoral research at Harvard, developed further and released by OpenAI as version 1.0 in July 2021) lets programmers write GPU kernels in Python at the level of tiles rather than threads, with the compiler handling details like shared memory and coalescing.
  - Specialized attention kernels such as FlashAttention (Tri Dao and colleagues, 2022) showed that careful attention to the memory hierarchy (tiling the attention computation so the full attention matrix never needs to be stored in global memory) could speed up transformers several-fold; this is the roofline lesson again (Chapter 18).

8. Parallelism across many GPUs

Large models need many GPUs. Main strategies:

  - Data parallelism: each GPU holds a copy of the model and processes a different part of the minibatch; gradients are averaged across GPUs with an all-reduce after each step. A ring all-reduce over P GPUs sends about 2 (P - 1)/P times the gradient size per GPU, nearly independent of P.
  - Model (tensor) parallelism: a single layer's matrices are split across GPUs.
  - Pipeline parallelism: different layers run on different GPUs, with microbatches flowing through like an assembly line.
  - Sharded data parallelism (such as ZeRO, 2019-2020): optimizer states, gradients and parameters are partitioned across GPUs to save memory.

Training the largest models of the 2020s combines all of these across thousands to tens of thousands of GPUs connected by high-bandwidth links (NVLink within a server, InfiniBand or Ethernet between servers). Communication bandwidth and latency, power and cooling become first-order engineering constraints, much like the wiring problems of the earliest computers (Chapter 4), at a vastly larger scale.

9. A mechatronics view

GPU programming concepts apply directly in robotics and embedded systems:

  - Embedded GPU modules (such as Nvidia's Jetson series) run CUDA for camera processing, neural network inference and point cloud processing on robots.
  - Image processing pipelines (undistortion, filtering, feature detection) map naturally to one thread per pixel.
  - Physics simulation for robot learning runs thousands of simulated robots in parallel on GPUs, enabling reinforcement learning at scale.
  - Real-time constraints: GPU kernels have launch overhead (microseconds) and data transfer costs, so for small, latency-critical control loops a CPU or microcontroller is often better; GPUs win on large, batched workloads.

10. Summary

  - CUDA, developed at Nvidia from 2004 (Ian Buck, John Nickolls and others) and public since 15 February 2007, made GPUs programmable in C-like code.
  - Kernels run as grids of thread blocks; threads in a block share memory and synchronize; blocks are independent, so programs scale across GPU sizes.
  - Warps of 32 threads execute in SIMT fashion; divergence costs performance; many warps hide memory latency.
  - Memory hierarchy (registers, shared memory, caches, global memory, host memory) and coalesced access dominate performance.
  - Tiling raises the arithmetic intensity of matrix multiplication by reusing data in shared memory.
  - cuBLAS, cuDNN (2014), NCCL and frameworks (Theano, Caffe, TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX) made GPUs accessible; Triton (2021) and fused kernels like FlashAttention (2022) push efficiency further.
  - Large-scale training combines data, tensor, pipeline and sharded parallelism across thousands of GPUs.
